summary:
Corrientes stands under Argentina's national framework for gender identity, health care, criminal law and document recognition; that national layer is assessed in the Argentina country record and is not restated here.

An April 2025 Washington Blade report, datelined Buenos Aires, names Corrientes among the more conservative interior provinces of Argentina where conditions for trans people are worse than in the capital. The characterisation comes from interviews with trans activists rather than from provincial government data, and the report attaches no Corrientes-specific incident, prosecution or policy to the province.

The same report records activists' accounts that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers, already present nationally, had worsened and was worst outside Buenos Aires. No figure, date or named case for Corrientes is given.

Emergency Decree 62/2025, issued 5 February 2025, bars under-18s from gender-affirming surgery and comprehensive hormonal treatment, and Decree 61/2025 changes how trans people are housed in the prison system. Both bind every province including Corrientes. FALGBT announced legal action and constitutional experts called the decrees unlawful; a Federal Court ruled the care ban unconstitutional in April 2025.

The Milei government also dismissed trans people hired under the 1% public-sector Trans Labor Quota and abolished the federal anti-discrimination agency INADI, removing a national complaint channel that residents of Corrientes had used.
tangentialFactors:
The Blade's placement of Corrientes among conservative interior provinces rests on activist interviews, not provincial data, so it indicates a perceived climate rather than a measured one.

No Corrientes-specific hate-crime count, prosecution or police-incident record appears in this inventory; the national hate-crime totals in the parent record are not disaggregated by province.
localsOnly:
Residents of Corrientes are subject to Decree 62/2025's under-18 care restrictions and Decree 61/2025's prison-placement rules, both of which bind the province directly.

Provincial police conduct toward trans and travesti sex workers is described by activists as among the worse outside Buenos Aires, but no Corrientes case, date or outcome is documented here.

INADI, previously a national route for discrimination complaints, was abolished, and trans public-sector workers hired under the Trans Labor Quota were dismissed; no Corrientes provincial replacement body is sourced.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Corrientes province has its own anti-discrimination ordinance, provincial trans-health protocol, or hate-crime reporting mechanism is not sourced in this inventory and remains unresolved.

No Corrientes-specific incident, arrest, court case or provincial policy document is available here; the province-level characterisation rests entirely on activist interviews in a Buenos Aires-datelined report.

The inventory does not record how Decree 61/2025 has been implemented in Corrientes prisons, nor whether any Corrientes detainee has been affected.
